standard.title: Plan reproducible investigations
standard.description: plan and conduct reproducible investigations to answer questions and test hypotheses, including identifying variables and assumptions and, as appropriate, recognising and managing risks, considering ethical issues and recognising key considerations regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can plan and conduct repeatable fair-test investigations, identifying variables (AC9S5I02). They have not yet planned for reproducibility, identified assumptions about controlled variables, or considered ethical issues and heritage site protocols.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students plan and conduct reproducible investigations, identifying variables and assumptions, recognising and managing risks, considering ethical issues and recognising heritage site considerations.

nodes.label: Variables and assumptions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify independent, dependent and controlled variables and recognise assumptions about controlled variables
nodes.minimum_width: Identify variables and at least one assumption in a provided investigation method; explain why controlling variables matters
nodes.typical_width: Identify independent, dependent and controlled variables and assumptions in a given method; explain what happens if an assumption is wrong; discuss why identifying variables and assumptions is important
wider: Identify assumptions relating to variables assumed to be constant, such as ambient temperature, material properties or substance purity
Compare two methods for the same investigation and evaluate which better controls variables
Design an investigation where an assumption about a controlled variable is deliberately tested

response_modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the three variable types or fail to recognise that controlled variables involve assumptions. These errors propagate directly into method design and evaluation. Seeing variable identification across different investigation contexts — forces, particles, ecosystems — helps students generalise the skill rather than memorising one example. Each new context forces fresh variable identification without the scaffold of familiarity.

success_criteria: Correctly identifies independent, dependent and controlled variables in a given method
Names at least one assumption about a controlled variable
Explains why controlling variables matters for the investigation

nodes.label: Planning reproducible methods
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can plan a method that another person could reproduce to obtain comparable results
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the features that make an investigation reproducible; compare a method with its hypothesis and assess whether it reasonably tests the hypothesis
nodes.typical_width: Plan a reproducible investigation method for a given hypothesis; have another student review it and identify gaps; revise based on feedback
wider: Limited width — writing reproducible methods is a precision skill that does not vary meaningfully across investigation types. All wider directions (multiple trials, peer review, explicit variable statements) are more practice on the same reproducibility criteria, not broader contexts.

response_modes.reason: Writing reproducible methods is a precision task — students commonly write methods that are too vague for someone else to follow. The skill does not vary meaningfully across contexts; what helps is practice writing, peer-testing and refining methods until sufficient detail becomes habitual. More investigation contexts don't help; more writing-and-feedback cycles do.

success_criteria: Plans a method with sufficient detail for another person to reproduce
Method logically tests the stated hypothesis
Peer review confirms the method is followable

nodes.label: Risks, ethics and heritage considerations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and manage risks, consider ethical issues and recognise heritage site protocols when planning investigations
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one risk in a given investigation and suggest how to manage it; identify one ethical consideration relevant to the investigation
nodes.typical_width: Identify risks and ethical considerations including interactions with living things; recognise state and territory laws relating to First Nations Australians' heritage sites and artefacts; integrate these into investigation planning
wider: Collaborate with First Nations Australians communities to plan investigations about ecosystems, ensuring mutually beneficial outcomes and following cultural protocols
Recognise First Nations Australians' artefacts and heritage sites and understand obligations not to harm or disturb sites
Design an investigation that explicitly addresses ethical issues relating to interactions with living organisms and justifies decisions made

response_modes.reason: Students commonly identify risks as a checklist item without reasoning through consequences — they name the risk without explaining what harm could occur or why the management strategy addresses it. Similarly, heritage considerations require explicit reasoning about obligation, not just recognition of existence. Scaffolding the reasoning (what could go wrong, who is affected, what is the protocol and why) builds genuine risk literacy rather than tick-box compliance.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The collaborative ecosystem investigation direction — working with First Nations communities to plan investigations with mutually beneficial outcomes — is genuinely rich. It introduces protocol, reciprocity, and community ownership of knowledge as dimensions of ethical investigation planning that go well beyond standard lab safety. Advancing students who engage this direction develop a more sophisticated understanding of what ethical research means.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one risk and suggests how to manage it
Identifies at least one ethical consideration relevant to the investigation
Recognises that heritage sites and artefacts require specific protocols
